title: Lou Singer, Earl Palmer and Manzie Campbell
summary: Jones tells how he introduced young drummers like Earl Palmer to Lou Singer and repeats that Manzie Campbell was the greatest he saw.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That's right, in California. I introduced all the little drummers out there. I had 55 drummers. I said I want you to meet Mr. Lou Singer. I had a little boy up there and I have the pictures to prove. His name is Earl Palmer. I said, "Earl, this is Mr. Lou Singer." He looked at Lou Singer like he's a shoeshine boy. I said, "Son, you better get with this man and learn. You know about Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich, and Shelly Manne and those people but you haven't scratched the surface. Why don't you go to this man and learn how to play?" See, because there was Lou Singer in all these people. You know what I'm talking about, Milt. You know how difficult it was to go down to the Loop to get a Coca-Cola. So now when the guys used to hang out together they could find out what they were doing. But the greatest drummer that I ever saw in my life in 51 years was Si Manzie Campbell. Now there was a drummer that played - a black man that looked like Jack Johnson and I will get from Bert Bacharach a picture of him - he looked like Jack and his name was Coach Johnson.
You mentioned him the other day.

You see, now this is circus and carnival now. You got to play something. There wasn't no test given to you. They just put the music up there and you went, but the naturalness and the flexibility these peoples have is something different.
